query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: The incorporation of in situ formed metastable ZrO2 particles into a high-entropy alloy (HEA) can enhance its toughness by inducing martensitic transformation and creating residual stress, which leads to crack deflection and bridging.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase high-entropy alloy (HEA) with a composition of (W0.2Ta0.2Nb0.2Zr0.2Ti0.2)C
generation.intervention: Incorporation of in situ formed metastable ZrO2 particles into the HEA
generation.conditions: Sintering pressure of 50 MPa, temperature of 1800 °C
generation.structural_mediator: Metastable ZrO2 particles with tetragonal and monoclinic crystal structures
generation.mechanism: Martensitic transformation of ZrO2 particles, residual stress, and crack deflection and bridging
generation.predicted_outcome: Enhanced toughness and fracture toughness of the HEA
generation.uncertainty: The exact mechanism of martensitic transformation and its effect on toughness, the optimal fraction and size of ZrO2 particles

falsification_experiment.design: Comparison of the mechanical properties of HEAs with and without ZrO2 particles, using techniques such as single edge notched beam (SENB) and indentation methods
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA with ZrO2 particles does not show enhanced toughness and fracture toughness compared to the baseline HEA, the hypothesis is falsified.
